PM edition, as of 2026-11-17 17:35 ET. Risk came off across the board into Nvidia's results. The S&P 500 fell 1.03% to 7340.53, the Dow dropped 1.64% (-848.75), the Russell 2000 lost 1.50% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.74%. Overseas it was worse: Euro Stoxx 50 -2.15%, FTSE 100 -1.76%, Nikkei -1.34%. VIX jumped 2.55 points to 25.46. Treasuries rallied modestly (10Y 5.1068%, -2.43bp; 2Y 4.8041%), gold was flat at 3850.1 and Brent rose 1.15% to 93.5. Compared with the prior session this is a step down: the S&P closed essentially on its 200-day average (computed distance -0.05%) and 4.11% below its 50-day. The biggest story under the surface is credit, where junk debt is split in two. The Bloomberg Caa–B gap is 772bp, against a 5-year average of 421bp. That puts it at the 98.98th percentile of the last five years and +189bp over three months, the widest since 2020-04-16; FRED's CCC–B gap of 972bp confirms it. So far that stress is not spreading up the ladder. Single-B moved -2bp over the month and BB -10bp, US IG OAS sits at 0.88% and HY OAS at 3.27%. Two early tells are worth watching. The B–Ba gap widened 14bp this week. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has climbed to 0.64 from 0.34 three months ago, though it is still below its 0.69 five-year median. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. On AI credit, CoreWeave's 5Y CDS is 1,170bp. That is 24bp under its 1,194.5bp Oct-15 record, holding 96.7% of the run up from the June low, and about 51bp tighter on the week. Nvidia's CDS was unchanged at 128.72bp. Neocloud equities kept falling: Nebius -24.3% and IREN -23.4% over the week. So the market is not pricing a broad failure of Nvidia's backstop, but it is not giving the neoclouds credit for it either. The tech-analog phase model keeps the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 29 days past peak with a basket drawdown of -20.28%. Two signposts have triggered. Breadth: 78.6% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs. AI infrastructure: the SOX is -34.3% from its 52-week high. The model's odds of ever reaching Phase 2 or worse within 12 months are 53.6%. The defensive dial stays at Step 1 – Cautious. Sentiment is fearful: the AAII bull–bear spread is -20.6pp and put/call is 0.73. Tonight's Nvidia print, the FOMC minutes this week and Anthropic's IPO debut (slated for Thursday) are the near-term swing factors.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.46 vol points (14th percentile of the 71 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 101.9 (74th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 86bp (steeper by 1bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 47 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 64/100 — Persistent and slowly firming, not re-accelerating sharply. The computed core-trend gauge (shown separately) has the underlying measures above the middle of their history, and most are rising. Median CPI 2.8% and 16% trimmed-mean CPI 2.9% are rising, median PCE 2.67% and trimmed-mean PCE 2.26% are flat, and core sticky CPI 3.06% is rising. Core PCE at 3.12% remains well above target. Breadth is the concern: in the Dallas distribution, 16.6% of the PCE basket is rising faster than 10% and another 10.2% at 5–10%, while 25.6% is falling. Flexible CPI at 6.2% (82nd percentile) reflects the energy shock. Market pricing is benign (5y breakeven 2.27%, 1y 1.97%), and wages are not the driver (AHE 3.1%, ECI 0.8%). Net: sticky core plus energy pass-through argues against easing and supports the Fed's hiking bias (persistence score is an analyst estimate).

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
8 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 6 beyond 2000 — 56/100
Today is past the froth peak and in the early stage of a bust, not at March 2000. On equity froth, the Nasdaq trailing P/E of 38.16x is only 14% of the way to the 2000 peak (175x), the Nasdaq trades 3.3% below its 200-day (0% of the 2000 run-up) and the SOX P/E is 32%. On late-cycle catalysts and macro regime, conditions are beyond 2000: IG tightness at 127%, Baa–10Y at 161%, NFCI looseness at 148% and commodities-vs-equities at 200%, with the curve at 69%. Signposts are washed out (AAII 0%, consumer confidence 31%, margin debt 40%), with VIX at 65%. The phase model places the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 29 days past the 2026-10-06 peak, with a basket drawdown of -20.28% (the same day in 2000 was -20.45%). It puts 6-month odds at P1 53.4%, P2 23.4%, P3 9.5% and P4 13.6%, and the chance of ever reaching Phase 2+ within 12 months at 53.6%; these are model estimates. Two signposts have triggered: breadth (78.6% of names more than 20% off their highs) and the SOX -34.3% from its high. The defensive step is 1 – Cautious.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (38x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analogy now works through credit, not valuation. Prices have already been cut hard: SMH -30.9%, Nvidia -34.7% and the neoclouds -63% to -76% from their highs. Meanwhile, credit spreads and financial conditions are looser than at the 2000 peak, which is what the bust phases punish. The model's path from Phase 1 to Phase 2 runs through HY OAS: 327bp now, against 420bp (5-year 80th percentile) and 448bp (Day-0 +150bp). The CCC stress and the CoreWeave CDS sitting near its record are where Phase 2 would start. The equity HMM regime is 82.2% 'volatile bull', and credit regimes are 97.2% calm. The model's historical tilt at this phase mix favored gold, Treasury duration and cash over mega-cap growth, international and EM. The rally watch shows spike-and-turn conditions flagged as on, with a 58.5% model chance of conditions within 5 days, but historically half of such rallies were traps (typical trap 12.5 days, +10.5%). My inputs (concentration ~37%, IPO froth ~75 driven by mega-IPOs like Anthropic, CAPE ~37x, market cap/GDP ~200%, LT EPS-growth expectations ~60) are analyst estimates, not verified quotes.

Odds the volatility-washout conditions line up within a week: 58%; within two weeks: 66%. Rallies of 8%+ that start in this phase: 50% later fail below their starting low (median 12 trading days, +10%); the rest become recoveries (median 130 days, +34%). Descriptive, not a signal.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and cash, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

⚔️Iran War

We could not find verifiable reporting on the Iran conflict dated after about November 5, 2026, so today's status is unconfirmed. As of early November: Iran said it was in 'intensive' indirect negotiations with the US through mediators (Qatar). A senior official offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington accepted Tehran's demands, including lifting the US naval blockade (Al-Monitor, Daily Sabah, Khaleej Times, Nov 1–3). Reports also said Iran would not reopen the strait until the US met seven conditions (Nov 5). On Nov 3–4, Trump confirmed a US strike on an Iranian anti-aircraft facility near Hormuz, and a maritime advisory rated the Hormuz threat 'severe'. Separately, Iran and Oman have discussed a temporary shipping corridor. Market read (analyst): Brent at 93.5 (+1.15% today) and a 1-month energy-sector decline of -6.93% suggest the market is pricing a stalled but not collapsing diplomacy track.

Sources: Khaleej Times – Iran says in 'intensive' negotiations with US to avert war via mediators · Al-Monitor – Iran gives 2-day window for Hormuz deal as US mulls strikes · Al Jazeera – Mediators continue US-Iran negotiations amid war rhetoric (Nov 1, 2026) · Daily Sabah – Iran offers to reopen Hormuz in 2 days as draft US deal circulates · ROIC – Iran refuses to reopen Strait of Hormuz until US meets seven conditions (11-05-2026) · The Citizen – Iran and Oman discuss temporary Hormuz corridor

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

December FOMC: a 25bp hike is the base case (analyst inference). At the October meeting the Fed held, with two dissents in favor of an immediate hike, and upgraded growth to 'strong'. Pre-meeting pricing was about 88% for a December hike, and Warsh named October and December as the key decision points (investinglive, Portfolio Adviser). A sharp market sell-off or a Nvidia/AI-credit shock is the main reason he might wait.

~1 YEAR

Analyst inference: one to two further hikes into 2027, consistent with market pricing of about 1.5 additional hikes (Portfolio Adviser). This would be paired with Warsh's long-held preference, on record before his tenure, for a smaller Fed balance sheet and less forward guidance (PIMCO). The Fed is also moving to a 6+2 meeting schedule, which means fewer scheduled decisions.

Warsh has avoided pre-committing ('won't prejudge rest of 2026') to keep his options open. With core PCE at 3.12%, sticky core CPI rising and the 10Y at 5.11%, his record as an inflation hawk who is skeptical of QE points to tightening rather than relief. Note that the sources conflict on the current policy range (3.75–4% vs 3.5–3.75%); we flag this rather than resolve it. We found no verified Warsh remarks dated this week. Pre-tenure pieces (Axios, PIMCO) that expected cuts are out of date.

Sources: Portfolio Adviser – Warsh sticks to the script as Fed holds rates but December hike highly likely · investinglive – Warsh won't prejudge rest of 2026, names October and December as decision points · investinglive – Fed chair Warsh talks up a storm but December rate hike bets barely budge · PIMCO – Under a Warsh Fed, expect a thoughtful policy approach · Axios – Kevin Warsh's challenges become clear after Powell's last hurrah
